draft.title: Sectarianism
card: Sectarianism is hostility or discrimination between religious groups who belong to the same wider faith. In Australia before 1945, the main divide was between Catholics and Protestants, both Christian.
Many Catholics were of Irish descent. Most colonial leaders and many settlers were Protestants, and some saw Catholics as less loyal to Britain.
The tension shaped politics, as parties and voters often lined up by religion. It shaped schools, as Catholics ran their own schools while public schools were mostly Protestant in tone.
It also shaped work, as some employers and workplaces favoured one group over the other. The tension continued into the 20th century.
draft.remember: Sectarianism was Catholic and Protestant tension that affected politics, schools and work.

a.q: Which situation is an example of sectarianism in Australia before 1945?
opts: An employer refuses to hire Catholics for jobs
A Catholic parish runs a fete for its church hall
A Protestant family moves from Sydney to Hobart
A Catholic and a Protestant study in one class
a.why: Refusing jobs because of a person's Catholic faith is discrimination between religious groups. Running a fete or moving house shows no hostility. Sharing a class is not sectarian by itself, as the tension lay in hostility or unfair treatment.
a.clue: Look for hostility or unfair treatment based on religion.

b.q: In 1920s Ballarat, Catholics fund their own parish school while nearby public schools teach mostly Protestant customs. Why does this show sectarianism shaping schools?
opts: The two groups were divided and kept separate schools
Catholics and Protestants shared one common school
Catholics and Protestants disagreed about Jewish teaching
Protestants had no religious beliefs about education
b.why: Separate schools show how the Catholic and Protestant divide shaped where children were taught. Sharing a school would show the opposite. Jewish teaching is not part of this divide, which was between two Christian groups.
b.clue: Think about which two groups were in tension, and how the schools were split.

a.best: An employer refuses to hire Catholics for jobs

b.best: The two groups were divided and kept separate schools

problems.detail: The clue 'how the schools were split' points straight at the only option about separate schools, so students can answer without understanding sectarianism.

Ballarat is in Victoria, where the Education Act 1872 made state schools 'free, compulsory and secular' and largely excluded religious instruction in school hours. Saying 1920s public schools there 'teach mostly Protestant customs' overstates it. 'Protestant in tone or ethos', as the card puts it, would be safer.

check.summary: The card and answers are sound. In question b, the clue gives the answer away, and saying 1920s Victorian state schools 'teach Protestant customs' overstates their secular status.

b.q: In 1920s Ballarat, Catholic families pay for their own parish school, as they see the nearby public school as Protestant in tone. What does this show?
opts: Sectarian division shaping how children were schooled
Tension between Christians and people of other faiths
Sectarian division shaping who was given work
Catholic families showing little interest in education
b.why: The Catholic and Protestant divide led Catholics to build their own schools, so it shaped schooling. It is not about work, as no one is being hired or refused a job. It is not about other faiths either, as both groups are Christian.
